## Napoleon

Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in 1799 and crowned himself Emperor in 1804. His Napoleonic Code standardized law across France—establishing equality before law, property rights, and secular authority. Military genius enabled conquest of most of Europe. He spread revolutionary ideals (meritocracy, legal equality) while imposing French dominance. The Continental System attempted to blockade Britain economically. Napoleon's invasion of Russia (1812) devastated his army. Defeated at Leipzig (1813) and exiled to Elba, he returned for the Hundred Days before final defeat at Waterloo (1815). Napoleon permanently reshaped European law, borders, and nationalism.

### Rise to Power

Napoleon Bonaparte (1769-1821) was born in Corsica, which had been acquired by France from Genoa just a year before his birth. Educated at French military academies, he was a brilliant student of mathematics, history, and military strategy. The Revolution provided opportunities for advancement that would have been impossible under the old regime's aristocratic military hierarchy, and Napoleon rose rapidly through the ranks.

His defense of the Convention against a royalist uprising in October 1795 (the famous "whiff of grapeshot") brought him to political prominence. His dazzling Italian campaign (1796-1797), in which he defeated the Austrians and created French client states in northern Italy, made him a national hero. His Egyptian expedition (1798-1799), though a military failure, demonstrated his ambition and his flair for self-promotion.

After his coup of 18 Brumaire, Napoleon consolidated power with remarkable speed and skill. The Constitution of Year VIII (1799) created a system of three consuls, but real power rested entirely with the First Consul — Napoleon himself. A plebiscite approved the new constitution by an overwhelming margin (though the vote was heavily manipulated). In 1802, Napoleon became Consul for Life. In 1804, he crowned himself Emperor of the French in a lavish ceremony at Notre-Dame Cathedral, taking the crown from Pope Pius VII and placing it on his own head — a gesture that symbolized his refusal to subordinate secular power to religious authority.

### The Napoleonic Code

The Napoleonic Code (Code Civil des Francais, 1804) was arguably Napoleon's most lasting achievement. Before the Code, France had no uniform legal system — northern France followed customary law, southern France followed Roman law, and local variations were innumerable. The Code established a single, coherent body of civil law for the entire nation.

The Code enshrined key revolutionary principles: equality before the law, freedom of religion, the abolition of feudal privileges, the protection of private property, and the secularization of the state. It established clear rules for contracts, property, inheritance, and family law. It guaranteed religious liberty and civil marriage.

However, the Code also reflected Napoleon's conservative social views. It strengthened patriarchal authority within the family — wives owed obedience to husbands, women could not enter into contracts or own property without their husband's consent, and divorce, while permitted, was made more difficult. It protected property rights above all other considerations, benefiting the bourgeoisie at the expense of the working poor.

The Napoleonic Code was exported throughout the French Empire and influenced legal systems across Europe, Latin America, the Middle East, and beyond. It remains the foundation of civil law in France and many other countries today.

### Military Campaigns and the Grand Empire

Napoleon was one of the greatest military commanders in history, winning a series of spectacular victories that gave France control of most of continental Europe by 1812. His military genius rested on speed, concentration of force, and the ability to exploit enemy weaknesses. He personally planned and directed campaigns with an attention to detail and a capacity for rapid decision-making that his opponents could rarely match.

The Battle of Austerlitz (December 2, 1805), in which Napoleon defeated the combined armies of Austria and Russia, is often considered his masterpiece — a perfect battle in which he manipulated his opponents into a trap and destroyed them. The battles of Jena-Auerstedt (1806) shattered the Prussian army. The Treaty of Tilsit (1807) with Russia briefly made France the dominant power in Europe.

At its greatest extent, the Grand Empire included France, the Low Countries, much of Germany and Italy, and parts of Spain, with satellite kingdoms ruled by Napoleon's relatives and allies. Napoleon reorganized the map of Europe, abolishing the thousand-year-old Holy Roman Empire, consolidating Germany's hundreds of states into a manageable number, and introducing the Napoleonic Code, meritocratic administration, and revolutionary principles throughout his domains.

### The Continental System and Economic Warfare

Unable to defeat Britain's naval supremacy (the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805 confirmed British control of the seas), Napoleon attempted to destroy Britain economically through the Continental System — a blockade that prohibited all European trade with Britain. The theory was that economic isolation would bankrupt Britain and force it to make peace.

The Continental System ultimately failed. It damaged European economies (which depended on British manufactured goods and colonial products) more than it damaged Britain. It bred resentment among Napoleon's allies and subjects. It provoked the disastrous Peninsular War in Spain (1808-1814), where Spanish guerrilla resistance and British intervention created a "running sore" that drained French military resources. And it contributed to the fatal decision to invade Russia.

### The Russian Campaign and Fall

Napoleon's invasion of Russia in June 1812 with a Grande Armee of over 600,000 men was the turning point of his career. The Russians refused to fight a decisive battle, instead retreating deeper into their vast territory, destroying everything in their path (scorched earth). When Napoleon finally reached Moscow in September, he found the city deliberately set ablaze. With winter approaching and no prospect of a peace treaty, Napoleon was forced to retreat.

The retreat from Moscow became one of the greatest military disasters in history. Harassed by Russian forces, decimated by cold, hunger, and disease, the Grande Armee was virtually destroyed. Fewer than 100,000 soldiers returned from Russia. The catastrophe encouraged Napoleon's enemies to form a new coalition, and at the Battle of Leipzig (October 1813), a combined force of Russians, Prussians, Austrians, and Swedes defeated him.

Napoleon abdicated in April 1814 and was exiled to the island of Elba. In March 1815, he escaped, returned to France, and rallied the army for the Hundred Days — a final bid for power that ended with his defeat at Waterloo (June 18, 1815) by British and Prussian forces under Wellington and Blucher. Napoleon was exiled to the remote island of Saint Helena in the South Atlantic, where he died in 1821.

### Legacy

Napoleon's legacy is among the most debated in Western history. He preserved key achievements of the Revolution — legal equality, meritocracy, religious tolerance, and rational administration — while destroying its democratic aspirations. He modernized European administration, law, and education, but at the cost of millions of lives and immense destruction. He spread revolutionary ideals across Europe, but also provocation of nationalist resistance movements that would reshape the continent.

The Napoleonic Code, the reorganization of Germany, the awakening of nationalism, and the principles of meritocratic governance all outlived Napoleon and shaped the 19th and 20th centuries. His career demonstrated both the creative and destructive potential of revolutionary energy channeled through military genius and personal ambition.

## Congress of Vienna

After Napoleon's defeat, European powers convened the Congress of Vienna (1814-1815) to restore order. Led by Austria's Metternich, the Congress sought to restore legitimate monarchies and maintain a balance of power. France was treated moderately to prevent resentment. The Concert of Europe established regular diplomatic meetings to prevent revolution and war. Conservative restoration suppressed liberal and nationalist movements. However, the Congress couldn't permanently contain the forces unleashed by the French Revolution. Liberalism (individual rights, constitutions) and nationalism (self-determination) continued to challenge the conservative order throughout the 19th century.

### The Post-Napoleonic Settlement

The Congress of Vienna was the most important diplomatic gathering in European history since the Peace of Westphalia (1648). Meeting from September 1814 to June 1815, it brought together representatives of virtually every European state to reconstruct the political order that Napoleon had demolished. The Congress was dominated by the "Great Powers" — Austria, Britain, Russia, and Prussia — represented by some of the most skilled diplomats of the era.

Prince Klemens von Metternich (1773-1859), Austria's foreign minister, was the dominant figure. A conservative aristocrat who feared revolution above all else, Metternich sought to restore the pre-revolutionary order and create mechanisms to prevent future upheavals. Viscount Castlereagh represented Britain, advocating for a balance of power that would prevent any single state from dominating Europe. Tsar Alexander I of Russia, influenced by both mystical Christianity and liberal ideas, played an unpredictable role. Karl August von Hardenberg represented Prussia. And Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand, representing defeated France, skillfully exploited divisions among the victors to secure surprisingly favorable terms for his country.

### The Principles of Vienna

The Congress operated on three guiding principles. The principle of legitimacy held that the "legitimate" monarchies overthrown by Napoleon should be restored to their thrones. The Bourbon dynasty was restored in France, Spain, and Naples. Legitimate rulers were reinstated across Italy and Germany. This principle served conservative interests by equating lawful authority with the pre-revolutionary order.

The principle of the balance of power sought to ensure that no single state could dominate Europe as France had under Napoleon. Territory was redistributed to strengthen potential counterweights to any future aggressor. The Netherlands was united with Belgium to create a buffer state on France's northern border. Prussia received the Rhineland (also bordering France) and part of Saxony. Austria gained Lombardy and Venetia in northern Italy. Russia retained Finland and most of Poland (as the Kingdom of Poland under the Russian tsar).

The principle of compensation ensured that the victorious powers received territorial rewards proportional to their contributions to Napoleon's defeat. This sometimes conflicted with the principle of legitimacy (territories were taken from legitimate rulers to reward allies), but pragmatic considerations generally prevailed.

### The Concert of Europe

The most innovative feature of the Vienna settlement was the Concert of Europe — an informal system of regular diplomatic consultation among the Great Powers. The idea was that periodic congresses and conferences would allow the powers to address crises collectively before they escalated into war. This was the first sustained attempt at international collective security in modern history.

The Concert system held several congresses in the years following Vienna — at Aix-la-Chapelle (1818), Troppau (1820), Laibach (1821), and Verona (1822). At Troppau, the reactionary powers (Austria, Prussia, and Russia) adopted the Troppau Protocol, claiming the right to intervene militarily in any country where revolution threatened the established order. Austria used this authority to suppress liberal revolts in Naples and Piedmont; France (with Allied approval) intervened to crush a liberal revolution in Spain in 1823.

Britain, however, increasingly distanced itself from the interventionist approach, opposing intervention in domestic affairs as a violation of national sovereignty. This divergence between the continental powers (committed to suppressing revolution) and Britain (committed to non-intervention and free trade) gradually weakened the Concert system.

### The Conservative Order and Its Challengers

Metternich's conservative order rested on three pillars: monarchy, aristocracy, and established religion. Metternich viewed liberalism and nationalism as interconnected threats to the multinational Habsburg Empire (which encompassed Germans, Hungarians, Czechs, Poles, Italians, Croats, Slovaks, Romanians, and others). If the principle of national self-determination were accepted, the Habsburg Empire would disintegrate. Liberal constitutions would limit aristocratic and monarchical power. Both tendencies threatened the social and political order that Metternich was determined to preserve.

Metternich's repressive measures included the Carlsbad Decrees (1819), which censored the press, dissolved liberal student organizations (Burschenschaften), and placed universities under surveillance throughout the German Confederation. Secret police monitored suspected liberals and nationalists. Political dissidents faced arrest, imprisonment, or exile.

Despite repression, liberalism and nationalism continued to grow. Liberals demanded constitutional government, individual rights, freedom of the press, and the rule of law. Nationalists sought self-determination for peoples defined by shared language, culture, and history. These two movements often overlapped — liberals tended to be nationalists, and nationalists tended to be liberals — and together they posed an existential challenge to the conservative order.

### Legacy and Assessment

The Congress of Vienna achieved its primary objectives with remarkable success. It prevented a general European war for nearly a century (until 1914), the longest period of relative peace in modern European history. It established mechanisms of international consultation that, while imperfect, moderated great-power competition and resolved several crises peacefully. The territorial settlement, while it satisfied no one completely, proved remarkably durable.

However, the Congress could not permanently suppress the forces of change. The revolutionary wave of 1820 challenged the conservative order in Spain, Naples, and Greece. The revolutions of 1830 overthrew the restored Bourbons in France and created an independent Belgium. The revolutions of 1848 swept across Europe, threatening the very foundations of the Vienna system. Italian and German unification in the 1860s-1870s completed the dismantling of the Vienna territorial settlement.

The Congress of Vienna thus represents both the greatest achievement of conservative diplomacy and its ultimate limitation: it could delay but not prevent the transformation of European politics by liberalism and nationalism. Its legacy — the concept of collective security, the pursuit of a balance of power, and the use of diplomacy to manage international competition — continues to influence international relations today.

## Italian & German Unification

Italy and Germany unified in the mid-19th century through a combination of nationalism, diplomacy, and war. Italian unification (Risorgimento) was led by Cavour's diplomacy in Piedmont-Sardinia, Garibaldi's military campaigns in the south, and Mazzini's nationalist ideology. Italy unified by 1870. German unification was orchestrated by Prussian Chancellor Bismarck through calculated wars against Denmark, Austria, and France. The German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles in 1871. Both unifications created powerful new nation-states that disrupted the European balance of power and fueled imperial competition.

### The Italian Risorgimento

The Italian unification movement (the Risorgimento, or "resurgence") was one of the most dramatic political transformations of the 19th century. Before unification, the Italian peninsula was divided into numerous states: the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia in the northwest, the Austrian-controlled Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia in the northeast, the Papal States across central Italy, the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in the south, and several smaller duchies and grand duchies. The Congress of Vienna had restored these divisions and Austrian dominance over the peninsula.

Three distinct visions of Italian unity competed for influence. Giuseppe Mazzini (1805-1872), the great ideologist of Italian nationalism, envisioned a democratic republic forged through popular revolution. His organization Young Italy inspired a generation of nationalist activists, and his romantic vision of a free, united Italy as a beacon of democratic civilization fired the imaginations of patriots throughout Europe. However, Mazzini's numerous attempts at revolutionary insurrection all ended in failure, demonstrating the limitations of ideology without military and diplomatic power.

Count Camillo di Cavour (1810-1861), the prime minister of Piedmont-Sardinia, pursued a very different strategy. A pragmatic liberal who admired British parliamentary government, Cavour sought to unite Italy under the Piedmontese monarchy through a combination of diplomatic maneuvering, economic modernization, and carefully limited warfare. He modernized Piedmont's economy, built railroads, liberalized trade, and created a constitutional government that made Piedmont the most progressive state in Italy.

Cavour's masterstroke was his alliance with Napoleon III of France against Austria. In the Franco-Austrian War of 1859, French and Piedmontese forces defeated Austria at the battles of Magenta and Solferino, liberating Lombardy. Revolutions in Tuscany, Parma, Modena, and the Romagna (all inspired by Cavour's agents) overthrew their rulers and voted for annexation to Piedmont. By 1860, northern and central Italy were united under the Piedmontese crown.

Giuseppe Garibaldi (1807-1882), a charismatic military leader and former follower of Mazzini, completed the unification from below. In May 1860, Garibaldi and his volunteer force of about 1,000 "Red Shirts" invaded Sicily, where they defeated the Bourbon army and liberated the island. Garibaldi then crossed to the mainland and swept northward, conquering Naples. In a dramatic meeting at Teano (October 1860), Garibaldi surrendered his conquests to King Victor Emmanuel II of Piedmont-Sardinia, subordinating his republican ideals to the goal of national unity under the monarchy.

The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in March 1861, with Victor Emmanuel II as king and Turin (later Florence, and finally Rome) as capital. Venetia was acquired from Austria in 1866 (as a result of the Austro-Prussian War). Rome was seized from the Pope in 1870, when the withdrawal of French troops (during the Franco-Prussian War) left the Papal States undefended.

### German Unification Under Bismarck

German unification was achieved through a very different process — one dominated by Prussian military power and the diplomatic genius of Otto von Bismarck (1815-1898). Before unification, the German-speaking world was organized in the German Confederation, a loose association of 39 states dominated by Austria and Prussia. The failure of the liberal Frankfurt Parliament (1848-1849) to achieve unification through democratic means convinced many Germans that national unity would have to be achieved through "blood and iron" — Bismarck's famous phrase.

Bismarck was appointed Minister-President of Prussia in 1862 by King William I, who needed a strong minister to overcome parliamentary opposition to army reform. Bismarck was a conservative Junker (Prussian landed aristocrat) who had no sympathy for liberalism or democracy. But he recognized that nationalism was a powerful force that could be harnessed to Prussian interests, and he pursued German unification — under Prussian leadership and on Prussian terms — through a series of brilliantly orchestrated wars.

The Danish War (1864) was fought ostensibly over the duchies of Schleswig and Holstein, which Denmark had attempted to incorporate into the Danish state. Prussia and Austria fought as allies, defeating Denmark and dividing the duchies between them. This set the stage for the next conflict.

The Austro-Prussian War (1866) was the decisive step. Bismarck engineered a diplomatic crisis over the administration of the conquered duchies, secured alliances with Italy and several smaller German states, and provoked Austria into war. Prussia's victory at the Battle of Koniggratz (Sadowa) in just seven weeks shattered Austrian power in Germany. The North German Confederation, dominated by Prussia, replaced the old German Confederation. Austria was excluded from German affairs.

The Franco-Prussian War (1870-1871) completed the process. Bismarck manipulated the crisis over the Spanish succession to provoke France into declaring war. The Ems Dispatch — Bismarck's edited version of a telegram describing a diplomatic exchange between the Prussian king and the French ambassador — was designed to humiliate France and make war inevitable. The French army was overwhelmed. Napoleon III was captured at the Battle of Sedan (September 1870). Paris fell after a four-month siege.

On January 18, 1871, in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles — a deliberate humiliation of France — the German Empire was proclaimed, with King William I of Prussia as Kaiser (Emperor). The new Germany was a federal state dominated by Prussia, with Bismarck as its first Chancellor. It was the most powerful state on the European continent, with the largest population, the strongest army, and a rapidly industrializing economy.

### Consequences

The unification of Italy and Germany fundamentally altered the European balance of power. Germany's emergence as a major industrial and military power created new tensions with France (which lost Alsace-Lorraine and sought revenge), Britain (which feared German naval expansion), and Russia (which competed with Germany for influence in the Balkans and Ottoman Empire). The alliance system that developed in response to German power — the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and the Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain) — created the diplomatic framework that led to World War I.

Italian unification, while achieving the goal of national unity, left many problems unresolved. The division between the industrialized north and the impoverished south (the "Southern Question") persisted. The Pope, stripped of his temporal territories, refused to recognize the Italian state, creating a rift between Church and state that lasted until the Lateran Accords of 1929. Irredentism — the desire to incorporate Italian-speaking territories still under Austrian control (Trentino, Trieste, Istria) — fueled Italian expansionist ambitions.

Both unifications demonstrated that nationalism, when combined with military power and diplomatic skill, could redraw the map of Europe. They also showed that the process of nation-building was never simply a matter of shared language and culture — it involved conquest, coercion, and the imposition of one state's authority over diverse populations who did not always welcome it.

## Revolutions of 1848

In 1848, revolutions erupted across Europe—France, the German states, Italian states, and the Habsburg Empire. Causes included economic depression, food shortages, and demands for liberal constitutions and national self-determination. France overthrew King Louis-Philippe and established the Second Republic. German liberals convened the Frankfurt Parliament seeking unification. Hungarian and Czech nationalists challenged Habsburg rule. Italian nationalists revolted against Austrian control. Most revolutions were ultimately suppressed by conservative forces and military power. However, they demonstrated the power of nationalism and liberalism, foreshadowing later successful unification and reform movements.

### Causes of the 1848 Revolutions

The revolutions of 1848 — the "Springtime of Peoples" — were the most widespread revolutionary wave in European history, erupting in over 50 countries and territories within a few months. Their causes were both structural and immediate.

The long-term causes included the growth of liberal and nationalist movements since the Congress of Vienna. Decades of conservative repression had created a pressure cooker of frustrated political aspirations. An expanding middle class demanded constitutional government, freedom of the press, and the right to political participation. National minorities within the multi-ethnic Habsburg, Ottoman, and Russian empires demanded self-determination. Workers and artisans, squeezed by early industrialization, demanded economic reform.

The immediate trigger was an economic crisis. The potato blight of 1845-1846 (the same one that caused the Irish Famine) devastated food supplies across Europe. A financial crisis in 1847 caused bank failures, business closures, and mass unemployment. Bread prices soared while wages fell. The combination of political frustration and economic desperation proved explosive.

### Revolution in France

The revolution began in France in February 1848. King Louis-Philippe, who had come to power in the Revolution of 1830 as a "citizen king," had grown increasingly conservative and had refused demands to extend the franchise beyond the wealthy elite. When the government banned a reform banquet in Paris, street demonstrations erupted. Louis-Philippe abdicated and fled to England. The revolutionaries proclaimed the Second Republic and established universal male suffrage, making France the first major European nation to grant the vote to all adult men.

The Second Republic was torn between moderate republicans, radical socialists, and conservative monarchists. The June Days of 1848 — a workers' uprising in Paris, brutally suppressed by the army with thousands killed — revealed the deep class divisions within the revolutionary movement. In December 1848, Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte (nephew of Napoleon I) was elected president on a platform of order and national glory. In 1851, he staged a coup d'etat and in 1852 proclaimed himself Emperor Napoleon III, ending the republic.

### Revolution in the German States

News of the February Revolution in Paris triggered uprisings throughout the German Confederation. In March 1848, liberal revolutionaries forced concessions from rulers in Prussia, Bavaria, Saxony, and numerous smaller states. An elected parliament, the Frankfurt Parliament, convened in May 1848 to draft a constitution for a united Germany.

The Frankfurt Parliament was dominated by liberal professionals — professors, lawyers, and journalists — who debated eloquently but lacked military power. They faced a fundamental dilemma: should a united Germany be "Greater Germany" (including Austria and its German-speaking territories) or "Lesser Germany" (excluding Austria and led by Prussia)? After months of debate, they opted for a Lesser Germany solution and offered the crown of a constitutional German Empire to King Frederick William IV of Prussia.

Frederick William rejected the offer, contemptuously calling it a "crown from the gutter" — he would not accept a crown offered by elected representatives rather than by his fellow monarchs. Without Prussian military support, the Frankfurt Parliament was powerless. By the summer of 1849, the Parliament had dissolved, its members dispersed, and the old order was restored. German liberals, disillusioned by the failure of democratic unification, increasingly looked to Prussian military power as the only realistic path to national unity — preparing the way for Bismarck.

### Revolution in the Habsburg Empire

The multi-ethnic Habsburg Empire experienced the most complex revolutionary upheaval. In Vienna, students and workers demanded a liberal constitution and forced Metternich — the architect of European conservatism — to resign and flee the country. Emperor Ferdinand was compelled to grant a constitution and summon a constituent assembly.

In Hungary, the charismatic liberal lawyer Lajos Kossuth led a movement for Hungarian autonomy, demanding a separate Hungarian government, parliament, and army. The March Laws of 1848 established a liberal constitutional government in Hungary, which went far toward making Hungary an independent state within the Habsburg framework.

In Bohemia (modern Czech Republic), Czech nationalists convened a Pan-Slav Congress in Prague, demanding autonomy and opposing German liberal nationalism, which they saw as a threat to Slavic national identity. The conflict between German and Czech nationalism within the Habsburg Empire illustrated the fundamental tension within the 1848 revolutions: the principle of national self-determination could pit one nationality against another.

In northern Italy, Milanese and Venetian revolutionaries rose against Austrian rule, and King Charles Albert of Piedmont-Sardinia declared war on Austria. The Italian campaign initially succeeded but ultimately failed when Austria reasserted its military superiority.

The Habsburg Empire survived the 1848 revolutions through a combination of military force and the exploitation of ethnic divisions. The Austrian army, led by Field Marshal Radetzky, defeated the Italian and Czech revolutions. In Hungary, the empire required Russian military assistance — Tsar Nicholas I sent 200,000 troops to crush the Hungarian revolution in 1849, an intervention that demonstrated the solidarity of conservative monarchies against revolution.

### Why the Revolutions Failed

The 1848 revolutions failed for several interconnected reasons. The revolutionaries were divided — liberals, nationalists, socialists, and democrats had different goals that often conflicted. Middle-class liberals feared working-class radicalism more than they feared conservative reaction. National movements competed with each other — German nationalists clashed with Czech and Polish nationalists; Hungarian nationalists oppressed Slovak and Romanian minorities. The conservative establishment retained control of the armies, and ultimately military force decided the issue.

The revolutionaries also lacked experienced leadership and practical political skills. Many were idealists — intellectuals, students, and professionals — who were better at articulating grievances than at building coalitions, managing institutions, or wielding power.

### Legacy

Despite their failure, the 1848 revolutions had lasting consequences. Serfdom was permanently abolished in the Habsburg Empire. Universal male suffrage was established in France (and the principle was increasingly accepted elsewhere). The failures taught important lessons: German and Italian nationalists concluded that unification required military power, not liberal parliamentarism — a conclusion that shaped the era of Bismarck and Cavour. The class conflicts revealed in 1848 fueled the growth of socialist and labor movements that would transform European politics in the following decades. And the principle of national self-determination, though defeated in 1848, proved impossible to suppress permanently — it would reshape the map of Europe in 1918 and again in 1989-1991.

## World Wars & Europe

WWI (1914-1918) devastated European civilization—10 million soldiers died in industrialized warfare. Empires collapsed (Ottoman, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, German). The Treaty of Versailles's harsh terms on Germany fueled resentment. The Great Depression enabled fascism's rise. WWII (1939-1945) caused 40+ million European deaths, including the Holocaust. Allied victory destroyed fascism but left Europe divided. The Marshall Plan rebuilt Western Europe. NATO and the Warsaw Pact formalized Cold War divisions. The wars ended European global dominance and shifted power to the US and USSR.

### The Causes of World War I

World War I was the product of a complex web of alliances, imperial rivalries, nationalist tensions, and miscalculations that transformed a regional crisis in the Balkans into a continental catastrophe. The underlying causes included the alliance system (the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy versus the Triple Entente of France, Russia, and Britain), an arms race (particularly the Anglo-German naval rivalry), imperial competition in Africa and Asia, and intense nationalism, especially in the multi-ethnic Balkans.

The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary by a Serbian nationalist in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, triggered a chain reaction of ultimatums, mobilizations, and declarations of war. Austria-Hungary, determined to punish Serbia, issued an ultimatum designed to be rejected. Russia mobilized in support of Serbia. Germany, honoring its alliance with Austria-Hungary, declared war on Russia and then on France. Britain entered the war when Germany invaded Belgium, violating its neutrality.

### The Experience of Total War

World War I was the first "total war" — a conflict that mobilized entire societies and blurred the distinction between soldiers and civilians. The Western Front, stretching from the English Channel to Switzerland, became a nightmare landscape of trenches, barbed wire, mud, and death. New technologies — machine guns, poison gas, artillery, tanks, and aircraft — made the battlefield unprecedentedly lethal. Battles like the Somme (1916), where 20,000 British soldiers died on the first day alone, and Verdun (1916), which produced nearly a million casualties, demonstrated the horrific cost of industrialized warfare.

The Eastern Front was more mobile but equally destructive. Russia suffered enormous casualties and economic dislocation that contributed to the revolutions of 1917. The Ottoman Empire's entry into the war extended the conflict to the Middle East, where the British conducted campaigns in Gallipoli, Mesopotamia, and Palestine. The sinking of the Lusitania and unrestricted submarine warfare eventually drew the United States into the war in 1917, providing the Allies with the manpower and resources to achieve victory.

### The Peace Settlement and Its Consequences

The Treaty of Versailles (1919) imposed harsh terms on Germany: loss of territory (Alsace-Lorraine to France, Posen and the Polish Corridor to Poland), military limitations (100,000-man army, no air force, no submarines), massive reparations payments, and the "war guilt clause" (Article 231), which forced Germany to accept sole responsibility for starting the war. Germans across the political spectrum viewed the treaty as unjust and humiliating. The resentment it generated contributed directly to the rise of Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party.

The war destroyed four empires — the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, and Ottoman — and created new nations (Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Finland, the Baltic states) based on the principle of national self-determination. The League of Nations, established to prevent future wars through collective security, proved ineffective because the United States refused to join and the organization lacked enforcement mechanisms.

### The Interwar Period and the Rise of Fascism

The interwar period was marked by political instability, economic crisis, and the rise of totalitarian ideologies. The Great Depression, which began with the Wall Street crash of October 1929, devastated European economies, creating mass unemployment, social desperation, and political radicalization. Democratic governments seemed unable to cope with the crisis, and authoritarian alternatives gained appeal.

Fascism emerged first in Italy, where Benito Mussolini established a dictatorship in 1922, and then in Germany, where Adolf Hitler was appointed Chancellor in January 1933. The Nazi regime rapidly dismantled democratic institutions, persecuted Jews and political opponents, rearmed Germany in violation of Versailles, and pursued an aggressive foreign policy aimed at creating a "Greater Germany" that would dominate Europe.

### World War II

World War II began with Germany's invasion of Poland on September 1, 1939. Hitler's blitzkrieg ("lightning war") tactics — combining tanks, aircraft, and mobile infantry in rapid, concentrated attacks — overwhelmed Poland in weeks, France in six weeks, and conquered most of continental Europe by 1941. Britain stood alone against Nazi Germany until Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union (June 1941) and Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor (December 1941) brought the USSR and the United States into the war.

The Eastern Front was the largest and most brutal theater of the war, where the Soviet Union bore the heaviest burden of fighting and dying. The Battle of Stalingrad (1942-1943), one of the bloodiest battles in history, marked the turning point. Soviet forces, at a cost of over a million casualties, encircled and destroyed a German army of 300,000 men. From Stalingrad onward, the Soviets drove westward, liberating occupied territories and eventually reaching Berlin.

The Western Allies invaded Normandy on D-Day (June 6, 1944), opening a second front that accelerated Germany's collapse. Hitler committed suicide on April 30, 1945, and Germany surrendered unconditionally on May 8, 1945 (V-E Day).

### The Holocaust

The Holocaust — the systematic murder of six million European Jews by the Nazi regime — was the most horrific crime in Western history. Beginning with legal discrimination (the Nuremberg Laws of 1935), escalating through ghettoization and mass shootings by the Einsatzgruppen on the Eastern Front, and culminating in industrialized genocide in extermination camps (Auschwitz, Treblinka, Sobibor, Belzec, Chelmno, and Majdanek), the Holocaust revealed the capacity of a modern, educated, technologically advanced society for systematic evil. The Nazis also murdered millions of Roma, disabled people, political prisoners, Soviet POWs, and others deemed racially or politically undesirable.

### The Postwar Settlement

World War II left Europe devastated and divided. An estimated 40 million Europeans died, including both military and civilian casualties. Cities lay in ruins. Economies were shattered. Millions of refugees and displaced persons wandered across the continent. The old European great powers — Britain, France, Germany, Italy — were exhausted and impoverished. Global power had shifted decisively to the United States and the Soviet Union.

The Marshall Plan (1948), through which the United States provided $13 billion in aid to rebuild Western European economies, was one of the most consequential acts of statesmanship in modern history. It restored economic prosperity, stabilized democratic governments, and bound Western Europe to the American-led international order. NATO (1949) provided collective military defense against the Soviet threat. Together, the Marshall Plan and NATO created the framework for Western European security and prosperity that persisted throughout the Cold War and beyond.

## Cold War Europe

Europe was divided by the Iron Curtain—democratic, capitalist West versus communist, Soviet-controlled East. The Berlin Wall (1961-1989) symbolized this division. Western Europe integrated economically through the European Coal and Steel Community (1951) and European Economic Community (1957). NATO provided collective defense. Eastern Europe experienced Soviet control, suppression of uprisings (Hungary 1956, Czechoslovakia 1968), and economic stagnation. Detente in the 1970s eased tensions. ## Greek Philosophy: Foundations of Western Thought

Greek philosophy represents one of the most consequential intellectual achievements in human history. Beginning in the sixth century BCE in the Ionian Greek colonies of Asia Minor, a small number of thinkers began asking fundamental questions about the nature of reality, knowledge, ethics, and governance—questions that continue to drive philosophical inquiry today. Their distinctive contribution was not merely the questions themselves (other civilizations asked similar questions) but the method: systematic rational argument, based on evidence and logic rather than myth, tradition, or religious authority.

### The Pre-Socratics: The Birth of Natural Philosophy

The earliest Greek philosophers, known as the Pre-Socratics, sought natural explanations for physical phenomena. Thales of Miletus (c. 624-546 BCE) proposed that water was the fundamental substance underlying all matter—a remarkable attempt to find unity behind the diversity of nature. Anaximander suggested an undefined infinite substance (the apeiron). Heraclitus argued that change was the fundamental reality ("you cannot step into the same river twice"), while Parmenides countered that change was an illusion and only unchanging Being was real.

Democritus (c. 460-370 BCE) proposed that all matter was composed of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms (atomos, "uncuttable"), moving through empty space. This atomic theory, remarkably prescient, was not confirmed experimentally until over two millennia later.

Pythagoras (c. 570-495 BCE) discovered the mathematical ratios underlying musical harmony and declared that "all is number"—the idea that mathematical relationships describe the deep structure of reality. This insight proved profoundly fruitful in the development of Western science.

### Socrates: The Examined Life

Socrates (c. 470-399 BCE) shifted philosophy from natural science to ethics and epistemology. He believed that the most important questions concerned how to live well and what constituted virtue, justice, and knowledge. His dialectic method—systematic questioning that exposed contradictions and forced deeper thinking—became the model for philosophical inquiry and is still used in legal education (the "Socratic method").

Socrates claimed to know nothing (Socratic irony) and saw himself as a gadfly, stinging the complacent Athenian establishment into critical self-examination. His statement that "the unexamined life is not worth living" encapsulates the philosophical commitment to reflective self-awareness that became central to Western intellectual culture.

His trial and execution in 399 BCE—by democratic Athens, on charges of impiety and corrupting youth—raised profound questions about the relationship between philosophy and politics, individual conscience and collective authority, that have never been fully resolved.

### Plato: The World of Forms

Plato (c. 428-348 BCE), Socrates's most famous student, founded the Academy in Athens and wrote philosophical dialogues that are masterpieces of both philosophy and literature. His central doctrine, the Theory of Forms, proposed that the physical world we perceive through our senses is merely a shadow of a higher, eternal, perfect reality—the world of Forms or Ideas. The Form of the Good, the highest Form, illuminates all others, much as the sun illuminates the physical world.

In the Republic, Plato described his ideal state, governed by philosopher-kings who had ascended from the darkness of ignorance (the Allegory of the Cave) to perceive the Forms directly. His political philosophy, while authoritarian by modern standards, raised fundamental questions about the relationship between knowledge and political authority, education and governance.

Plato's influence on Western civilization is incalculable. His distinction between appearance and reality shaped Christian theology (through Augustine's synthesis of Neoplatonism and Christianity), medieval philosophy, early modern rationalism, and continues to influence debates about the nature of mathematics, morality, and knowledge.

### Aristotle: Empiricism and Classification

Aristotle (384-322 BCE), who studied at Plato's Academy for twenty years before tutoring Alexander the Great and founding his own school (the Lyceum), was arguably the most influential thinker in Western history. Where Plato looked upward to transcendent Forms, Aristotle looked around at the empirical world, observing, classifying, and analyzing.

Aristotle virtually invented formal logic, creating the system of syllogistic reasoning that dominated Western thought until the 19th century. He classified the natural world with extraordinary thoroughness—his biological works, based on systematic observation of hundreds of species, were not surpassed until the modern era. He established the fields of physics, metaphysics, ethics (Nicomachean Ethics), politics (comparing 158 constitutions), rhetoric, poetics, and psychology as distinct disciplines.

His ethical theory centered on eudaimonia (flourishing, well-being) achieved through the practice of virtues—character traits that represent the mean between extremes of excess and deficiency (courage is the mean between recklessness and cowardice). This "virtue ethics" has experienced a major revival in contemporary philosophy.

### The Legacy

Greek philosophy's commitment to rational inquiry, evidence-based argument, and systematic thinking became the intellectual foundation of Western civilization. Its questions—What is real? What can we know? How should we live? How should we be governed?—remain the central questions of philosophy, science, and political theory today.

## Renaissance Art & Humanism

The Italian Renaissance (roughly 1350-1550) was one of the most creative periods in Western history, producing revolutionary developments in art, architecture, literature, and thought. At its heart was humanism—an intellectual movement that recovered and celebrated classical Greek and Roman culture while placing human experience, potential, and achievement at the center of cultural life. The Renaissance did not reject Christianity, but it expanded the scope of human inquiry beyond purely theological concerns, creating a cultural climate that valued individual creativity, empirical observation, and earthly accomplishment alongside spiritual salvation.

### The Origins of Humanism

Humanism began as a literary and educational movement in 14th-century Italy. Petrarch (1304-1374), often called the "father of humanism," devoted his life to recovering, editing, and imitating classical Latin texts. He loved Cicero's elegant prose and Virgil's poetry, and he believed that the study of classical literature—the studia humanitatis (grammar, rhetoric, history, poetry, and moral philosophy)—could improve human character and civic life. This was not merely an academic exercise: humanists believed that exposure to the wisdom and eloquence of the ancients would produce better citizens, better leaders, and better human beings.

The movement grew through the 15th century, centered in Florence but spreading to Rome, Venice, Milan, and beyond. Humanist scholars scoured monastic libraries for forgotten manuscripts, established critical methods for dating and authenticating texts, and developed a command of classical Latin (and eventually Greek and Hebrew) that allowed direct engagement with ancient sources.

### Florence and the Medici

Florence was the epicenter of the Renaissance, and the Medici family was its greatest patron. Cosimo de' Medici (1389-1464) used his banking fortune to support artists, architects, and scholars. His grandson Lorenzo the Magnificent (1449-1492) presided over a court that included some of the greatest minds of the age. Medici patronage was partly civic pride (glorifying Florence), partly personal ambition (demonstrating cultured magnificence), and partly genuine intellectual passion.

The Florentine system of competitive patronage, where wealthy families and institutions vied to commission the most impressive works, created an environment of extraordinary creative energy. Artists were valued as never before in Western history—they moved from the status of anonymous craftsmen to celebrated creative geniuses.

### Revolutionary Art: From Giotto to the High Renaissance

The artistic revolution of the Renaissance unfolded over two centuries. Giotto (c. 1267-1337) broke with the flat, stylized Byzantine tradition by painting figures with three-dimensional weight and human emotion—his frescoes in the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua are considered the first great works of Renaissance art.

Brunelleschi (1377-1446) solved the engineering challenge of building the dome of Florence Cathedral (the largest masonry dome ever constructed) and developed the mathematical principles of linear perspective, which allowed artists to create the illusion of three-dimensional space on a flat surface. This was a revolutionary technique that transformed Western art.

The High Renaissance (c. 1490-1527) produced three supreme masters. Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519) was the prototypical "Renaissance man"—painter, sculptor, engineer, anatomist, inventor, and scientist. His Mona Lisa and Last Supper are among the most famous paintings in history. His notebooks, filled with drawings and observations of anatomy, engineering, and nature, reveal a mind of extraordinary range and originality.

Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475-1564) was a sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of titanic ambition. His David (1501-1504) embodies the Renaissance ideal of human beauty and power. His ceiling frescoes in the Sistine Chapel (1508-1512)—depicting the Creation, the Fall, and the Flood—are considered one of the supreme achievements of Western art. His design for St. Peter's Basilica in Rome, including its iconic dome, defined the architectural skyline of the Catholic world.

Raphael (1483-1520), though he died at thirty-seven, produced works of serene beauty and compositional mastery. His School of Athens, a fresco in the Vatican depicting the great Greek philosophers gathered in dialogue, is a visual manifesto of Renaissance humanism.

### Machiavelli and Political Thought

Niccolo Machiavelli (1469-1527) applied the humanist spirit of empirical inquiry to politics. His most famous work, The Prince (1513), analyzed power with ruthless realism, arguing that effective rulers must be willing to use deception, force, and manipulation when necessary. Often condemned as immoral, Machiavelli was actually pioneering the study of politics as it actually works rather than how it ideally should work. His separation of political analysis from moral philosophy was a founding moment of modern political science.

### Architecture and Urban Design

Renaissance architects drew on classical Greek and Roman models: columns, arches, domes, symmetry, and mathematical proportion. Brunelleschi, Alberti, Bramante, and Palladio created buildings of harmonious beauty that expressed humanist ideals of order, reason, and human dignity. Palladio's villas in the Veneto region influenced architecture from Inigo Jones in England to Thomas Jefferson's Monticello.

### The Significance of the Renaissance

The Renaissance did not create modernity single-handedly, but it prepared the ground. By recovering classical knowledge, developing new artistic techniques, celebrating individual achievement, and applying rational analysis to politics and nature, Renaissance thinkers and artists expanded the boundaries of what Western civilization believed humans could accomplish. Their confidence in human potential—expressed in Pico della Mirandola's famous Oration on the Dignity of Man (1486), which declared that humans could choose to ascend to the divine or descend to the bestial—remains a defining feature of Western culture.

## The Protestant Reformation

The Protestant Reformation, launched by Martin Luther's 95 Theses in 1517, shattered the religious unity of Western Christendom and reshaped European politics, culture, and society in ways that continue to reverberate today. What began as a theological dispute about the selling of indulgences became a revolution that challenged papal authority, created new churches, provoked devastating wars, and ultimately contributed to the development of modern individualism, religious pluralism, and the separation of church and state.

### Background: The Late Medieval Church

The Reformation did not emerge from nowhere. For centuries, critics had attacked corruption in the Catholic Church: the sale of ecclesiastical offices (simony), absenteeism (bishops who collected income from their dioceses but never visited), clerical immorality, and excessive papal taxation. Pre-Reformation movements—the Waldensians, John Wycliffe's Lollards in England, and Jan Hus's followers in Bohemia—had challenged Church authority and called for reform, but the Church suppressed them.

By 1500, the papacy had become deeply worldly. Renaissance popes like Alexander VI and Julius II behaved more like Italian princes than spiritual leaders—waging wars, fathering children, and spending lavishly on art and architecture. Pope Leo X's need to finance the construction of St. Peter's Basilica in Rome led him to authorize the aggressive sale of indulgences in Germany—the immediate trigger for Luther's protest.

### Martin Luther's Challenge

Martin Luther (1483-1546), an Augustinian monk and professor of theology at the University of Wittenberg, experienced a profound spiritual crisis. Tormented by his sense of sinfulness and inability to earn salvation through good works, he found consolation in Paul's Epistle to the Romans: "The just shall live by faith." This insight became the foundation of his theology: salvation comes through faith alone (sola fide), by God's grace alone (sola gratia), as revealed in Scripture alone (sola scriptura).

When the Dominican friar Johann Tetzel arrived near Wittenberg selling indulgences with the slogan "As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs," Luther was outraged. On October 31, 1517, he posted his 95 Theses challenging the theological basis of indulgences on the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg. The theses, originally intended for academic debate, were translated into German and distributed by the printing press across Germany within weeks—the first viral media event in history.

### The Break with Rome

Luther's challenge escalated rapidly. In a series of powerful treatises in 1520, he rejected papal authority, called for the German princes to reform the Church, argued that all believers were priests (the priesthood of all believers), and attacked the sacramental system, reducing the seven sacraments to two (baptism and communion). He also rejected monasticism, clerical celibacy, and the doctrine of transubstantiation (replacing it with consubstantiation).

Pope Leo X excommunicated Luther in January 1521. Emperor Charles V summoned Luther to the Diet (assembly) of Worms, where Luther reportedly declared: "Here I stand; I can do no other." Frederick the Wise of Saxony protected Luther by "kidnapping" him and hiding him in Wartburg Castle, where Luther translated the New Testament into German—making Scripture directly accessible to ordinary Germans for the first time.

### The Spread of Lutheranism

German princes had both religious and political reasons to support Luther. Adopting Lutheranism allowed them to seize Church lands and wealth, assert independence from the Emperor (who supported the Pope), and gain control over religious affairs in their territories. The Peace of Augsburg (1555) established the principle cuius regio, eius religio ("whose realm, his religion")—each prince could determine the religion of his territory.

### The Reformation's Broader Impact

The Reformation had consequences far beyond theology. It promoted literacy (so believers could read Scripture). It challenged traditional authority and hierarchies (contributing to later democratic movements). It stimulated the development of national languages and national identities. It created a culture of individual conscience and personal responsibility before God that influenced the development of modern individualism. And it provoked religious wars that devastated Europe for over a century, eventually leading to the principle of religious toleration—not because Europeans became tolerant, but because they exhausted themselves fighting.

The Reformation permanently divided Western Christianity into Catholic and Protestant branches and set in motion the modern Western commitment to religious pluralism, individual conscience, and the questioning of established authority.

## Napoleonic Wars & the Congress of Vienna

Napoleon Bonaparte (1769-1821) was one of the most consequential figures in Western history. Rising from minor Corsican nobility to become Emperor of France and master of most of Europe, he spread revolutionary ideals of legal equality, meritocracy, and rational administration while simultaneously imposing French domination through military conquest. The Napoleonic Wars (1803-1815) reshaped the political map of Europe, destroyed the remnants of the medieval order, and provoked a conservative reaction—the Congress of Vienna system—that attempted to restore stability but could not permanently suppress the revolutionary forces Napoleon had unleashed.

### Napoleon's Rise to Power

Napoleon Bonaparte rose through the ranks of the French Revolutionary army, demonstrating extraordinary military talent in campaigns in Italy (1796-1797) and Egypt (1798-1799). In November 1799, he seized power through a coup d'etat, overthrowing the ineffective Directory and establishing himself as First Consul. In 1804, he crowned himself Emperor of the French in a ceremony at Notre-Dame Cathedral, taking the crown from Pope Pius VII's hands and placing it on his own head—symbolizing that his power derived from himself and the French people, not from the Church.

### The Napoleonic Code

Napoleon's most enduring achievement was not military but legal. The Napoleonic Code (Code Civil, 1804) standardized French law, replacing the patchwork of feudal customs, royal edicts, and regional codes with a single, clear, rational legal system. Its key principles included: equality before the law (abolishing aristocratic legal privileges), protection of private property, freedom of religion, the right to choose one's profession, and secular civil authority over marriage and family law.

The Code spread wherever Napoleon's armies went—Belgium, the Netherlands, the Rhineland, Italy, Spain, and Poland. It became the basis for legal systems across continental Europe, Latin America, and parts of Asia and Africa. It remains the foundation of French law today and is considered one of the most influential legal documents in history.

### Military Campaigns and the Grand Empire

Napoleon's military genius lay in his ability to concentrate forces rapidly at the decisive point, using speed, surprise, and overwhelming force to destroy enemy armies in pitched battle. His victories at Austerlitz (1805, against Austria and Russia), Jena (1806, against Prussia), and Wagram (1809, against Austria) made him master of continental Europe. By 1810, his Grand Empire included France, Belgium, the Netherlands, western Germany, northern Italy, and much of Spain, with allied or satellite states covering most of the rest of the continent.

Napoleon spread revolutionary reforms wherever he conquered: feudal privileges were abolished, religious toleration was established, careers were opened to talent rather than birth, and rational administration replaced aristocratic governance. However, French domination also meant heavy taxation, conscription of local men into the French army, and economic subordination to French interests. This combination of liberation and exploitation stimulated national consciousness across Europe—people absorbed revolutionary ideals of equality and self-determination, then turned those ideals against French domination.

### The Defeats: Russia and Waterloo

Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812 was catastrophic. His Grande Armee of over 600,000 men entered Russia in June. The Russians refused pitched battle, retreating and destroying everything in Napoleon's path (scorched earth policy). Napoleon captured Moscow in September, but the city had been evacuated and set ablaze. With winter approaching and no food or shelter, Napoleon ordered a retreat that became one of the worst military disasters in history. Fewer than 100,000 men survived the march back.

Emboldened, a coalition of European powers defeated Napoleon at the Battle of Leipzig (1813, the "Battle of the Nations") and invaded France. Napoleon abdicated and was exiled to the island of Elba. He escaped in March 1815 for the Hundred Days but was definitively defeated at the Battle of Waterloo (June 18, 1815) by British forces under Wellington and Prussian forces under Blucher. He was exiled to the remote island of Saint Helena in the South Atlantic, where he died in 1821.

### The Congress of Vienna (1814-1815)

After Napoleon's defeat, representatives of the major European powers—Austria (led by the brilliant diplomat Metternich), Britain (Castlereagh), Russia (Tsar Alexander I), and Prussia (Hardenberg)—gathered in Vienna to reconstruct the European order. France was represented by Talleyrand, who skillfully prevented harsh punishment.

The Congress operated on several principles. Legitimacy meant restoring the "legitimate" monarchies that Napoleon had overthrown (the Bourbons in France, Spain, and Naples). Balance of power meant ensuring that no single state could dominate Europe as France had. Compensation meant redrawing borders to reward the victors and create buffer states around France.

### The Concert of Europe

The Congress created the Concert of Europe, a system of regular diplomatic conferences where the great powers would consult on European affairs and intervene collectively to suppress revolution and maintain the status quo. This system maintained relative peace in Europe for nearly forty years (the "Long Peace," 1815-1853) and represented the first sustained attempt at international collective security.

### Legacy and Limitations

The Congress of Vienna was remarkably successful on its own terms: it prevented a general European war for a century (until 1914). However, it could not permanently suppress the forces of liberalism (individual rights, constitutional government) and nationalism (self-determination of peoples) that the French Revolution and Napoleon had unleashed. Revolutions in 1820, 1830, and 1848 challenged the conservative order. Italian and German unification (1859-1871) overthrew the balance established at Vienna. The tension between conservative order and revolutionary change remained the central dynamic of 19th-century European politics.
